title: The Barrow Roll of Hollin
author: begun by Orm Hollin, Barrow Reeve, and continued in his hand for rather longer than that
body:
# The Barrow Roll of Hollin

*Kept in the Bell Cist. Read at the turn of each season, aloud, by the Reeve.*

---

**Orm Hollin**, Reeve of this ground, who dug the first cist and lay down in the fourth.

**Maud Hollin**, his wife, buried with her own shears and a loaf, the loaf being custom and the shears being hers.

**Ansel Hollin**, seven years, buried with a wooden bell.

*(Here forty-one lines, each a name, each with the tool it went down holding: a billhook, a shepherd's crook, three ladles, a mason's square, a bee-skep, an eel-knife brought up from the Mere, a fiddle.)*

---

## The second hand, which is the same hand

**Larkstead.** Fourteen hearths. The whole village, in the winter of 993, brought down the lane on carts by nobody, because there was nobody left in Larkstead to bring them. I have written the fourteen names I could find cut on their doorsteps. I have written *and others* under them, and I am ashamed of the line and I will not scratch it out.

**Gosford.** Nine hearths. Not here. Not anywhere. I walked it in 981 and again in 982 and there is a green and a lane and no ground that has been opened.

---

## What a Reeve is for

A Warden's Roll says a place is still under its name. This roll says a person is still under this ground. They are the same work and the Rest has forgotten that it split off from us, and I have stopped writing letters about it.

The reading is the whole of the office. Not the digging; anybody can dig. A hundred and forty names at the turn of a season takes a little over forty minutes and it must be done aloud, because a name read in the head is a name thought about, and thinking about a thing is not the same as saying it where the air can carry it.

I am past being able to say who has been reading them lately. I know that they are read. I know that the bell in this cist is the only warm thing in the ground and that it was hung by somebody who understood what warmth is for.

If you have this roll in your hands and you are breathing, then I have stopped, and forty minutes of your season belongs to a hundred and forty people who are not in a position to ask.

title: The Figures: a held breath, nightly, forty-one years
author: Ismay Ondrael, Sayer of the Breath, who is the instrument and says so on the first page
body:
# The Figures

*Four columns: the date, the hour, the glass-count, the room. Kept nightly since Y.T. 1002. The fourth column was added in the ninth year, for reasons given below.*

---

## The first page, written last

If the world is being breathed in, breath itself may be shortening, and nobody has ever taken the measurement. So: one glass, one set of lungs, one hour of an evening, for as long as I last.

The result, stated plainly and not published: **it is shorter.** By rather more than a woman going from three years old to forty-four should account for. Not enough to be certain. Certainly enough to be frightening.

I have not published it and I have been asked twice why not, and the answer is the fourth column.

## The fourth column

In the ninth year I noticed that the figure was low in my own cell and high in the refectory, and that I had been taking it in my own cell for nine years. So I began to write down the room.

The figure is longest in a warm room with people talking in it. It is shortest in a cold room by myself. The difference between those two is larger than the difference between me at thirty and me at forty-four.

This is a ruinous result for my own account and I have set it down in the middle of my own book. If the Breath were taking the world's air, the room would not matter. The room matters more than the year.

## Why the instrument cannot publish

Because the instrument is frightened, and a frightened instrument reads low, and I cannot subtract my own fear from a column of my own figures.

What is wanted is somebody young and unfrightened to take the same glass into a warm room and a cold one and write the figures in their own hand, so that the result is not mine. I have said this in three lectures. Nobody has offered.

*(Below, in a second and much newer hand, the figures from a warm inn on a market night and from a bell-hall under a city, twenty paces from running water, with nobody talking.)*
